review_text:
A decent 3D point and click adventure game if gotten on sale. There's an entertaining B movie horror plot to play out here, the passion of the developers showing in the melodramatic build ups and loving focus on the kill shots. It's just a shame the gameplay built around this is threadbare.

Lucius stars the unambiguously evil Antichrist, a six year old boy awakening to his calling of murdering those around him to fuel his new power. The entire game takes place inside the spacious family mansion as your father's senatorial campaign begins to collapse due to the strange murders at his home, the world's most incompetent police vaguely consider doing something about it and all the staff stay on well past the point of good sense. Classic camp. It's an entertaining one and done almost all the way through.

You're guided to your murder of the day and explore the mansion to pick up things for the occasional clever kill. You wander around, it's a big place, the mansion has a lot of heart even if it's not the best level design. Lots of good set pieces never used for the entire game like the library/billiards room. Sometimes you get a healthy amount of tips and are pointed in a good direction, there's a set of optional little chores you can do to get presents that'll help you. One gives a vague hint for the chapter, the other highlights interactables and should be an infinite use base ability for this kind of game. It's fun to run around and explore the mansion... for a time. Realizing that every drawer in the game can be opened but only one has anything deflates the map design a bit. The murders themselves are simple puzzles and ideally between the music box, in-game hints and spending some time on observation you can piece together what you're supposed to do. If not you wander around aimlessly growing bored. This is definitely a title where playing with a guide might save you headaches, or at least giving each stage a fair go for 15-30 minutes and looking up the answer as last resort. Lucius can devolve to pixel hunting and nothing highlights easily, especially with the dodgy power targeting.

There's strictly one correct way to do everything in the game and that undermines the appeal of the sandbox. You get powers though they're either far too limited in what they do or are used so liberally they undermine the creative puzzle-solving. One particularly good stage is framing somebody for your crimes while also providing enough emotional shock to make them a sobbing wreck, allowing you to mind control them to suicide. Good set up, good execution, fun premise, practical addition to the story, love it. Another is filler: you place a loaded gun next to somebody and mind control them to kill themselves. Considering Lucius can fire the gun himself that's not a clever murder, it's a regular one with extra steps. Combustion can only be used at very specific plot mandated points, Memory Wipe is just a get out of mistakes free card instead of an actual thing for setting up ironic suicides. Why not have a scenario where I can make somebody forget what they're doing like mixing medication or cooking with something volatile and make them double dose it? Mind Control people to start fights with one another and sneak in an escalating murder tool? Start small fires? Alternative kills could justify a second playthrough.

Lucius is decent. It has heart. I think the charming cheesiness of the story carries it but at the end of the day this game could've gone a bit further. The only really bad bits are the combat and the almost complete absence of the stealth mechanics. If you get seen, memory wipe. If you're in a stealth section, redo it and pray it ends soon. There aren't any actual threats for most of the game and perhaps the police and priests should've been an acting roaming danger, escalating at each new third of the game. 

And for the record it's not 20 hours of game, definitely not 40 hours of game. Nice try, achievements. There's no reason to replay it since the paths are so strict. As it is Lucius is a really nice $2 game. It's almost worth the $10 asking price but I recommend you get Lucius on sale for a decent 3-4+ hours of macabre fun.

So remember when we were all wishing to play a game where we are the bad guys, and all we got was a funny comedy game called Overlord, where we played as somewhat of a bad guy but not really.. Well this game you are the bad guy,, err bad kid.. you go around, plotting and murdering people.. watching people have sex, and seeing nudity.. it's one of those games that will leave you feeling kind of dirty...

Gameplay,

you play various chapters where you can set up elaborate traps to kill employees of your wealthy parents and anyone else who gets in your way including your own family,... Whether it's locking them in a freeze, putting them in the oven, poison, gunshots, crossbows,, you're in the words of Samuel L Jackson a BAMF....

The game takes place in third person, you pick up various items, combine them, and then use them on various objects.. most of the time the kills are very straightforward, and the game pretty much only gives you one way to kill the person but you're normally given a few extra task during the game, whether it's cleaning up your room, to finding pictures etc etc etc... Although most stages are fairly large and give you lots of freedom, the actual chapters normally only require you to move around a few rooms, collect 4 or 5 items and then get a really satisfying kill.

Also has a Tricycle you can ride around on like a Pimp, while you plan and carry out your killing sprees,, Don't forget to turn those crosses upside down,, nothing worst then getting ready to set someone on fire only to find out that Cross chilling a foot away from them drained you of power like that time Lance Armstrong forget his injection..

Lucius is a horror game in a sort of Hitman style where you play as a kid trying to kill members of your house in an effort to please your father, the Devil, and make them all look like accidents. It sounds super cool and then you play it and see that everything can only really happen one way and after the first 2 kills it can get incredibly confusing. You'll have to start pulling elaborate tricks to get people into positions in time for certain things. One specific one I remember had me grabbing a cassette, breaking a washer so one guy would leave, the cassette made the other move, grabbing paint thinner and a cloth, knocking the cassette guy out with those two after combining them, turning on the car with telekinesis, and then mind controlling the first guy into disabling the air conditioning so that the fumes would kill cassette guy. This led into a comically easy kill on washer guy where you burn him to death.

The story of Lucius is stupidly simple and won't change your life or anything. The story IS the premise, and that's all you really need to know.

I really like the environment the game takes place in. It's a decently realistic house even if it feels pretty video game-esque. There are tags next to rooms that tell you what room you're at, symmetrical house with mirrored layouts for each side, and for some reason, the doors are locked at the beginning. This was really weird given that it limits exploration and learning the house and also makes no sense from a story perspective why doors in your own house would be locked.

Animations and models show their age pretty harshly here. The main character has a mean case of potato face and everyone just kinda looks...mushy, for lack of a better word. This is a problem with the other Lucius games as well, especially the 3rd one though. Voice acting is also incredibly rough in some areas and surprisingly great in others. I thought the voice actor for Jack McGuffin did a pretty excellent job.

I actually didn't have many bugs at all while I was playing which is crazy since I heard this whole franchise was bug crazy but I never experienced any in this game. That doesn't mean you won't though, so that's just my own experience.

Lucius is a confusing mess of a puzzle adventure game. There isn't much room to do things differently and I don't really see replay value factoring in much, but I still had a pretty good time and would recommend it to someone who might've liked Hitman or games of that nature. Just don't expect it to be as open ended as Hitman is though, because it definitely isn't.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

Look, I know y´all love this game. But as much as I like it just like the next guy in the line, I gotta break it to you- Lucius aged like a fine milk. 

The promises of unbridled rampage went unfullfilled. Sure, the executions are brutal, BUT THERE IS ONLY ONE WAY IN WHICH YOU CAN DO THEM. It´s a shame, because it´s somewhat of an open world game, with memorable deaths no less.

But, what would wake this game even more memorable is if you were able to execute people in many ways. This is just an idea, but listen:
The more supernatural murder method you choose, the more crosses get put up around the house, hindering your abilities later in the game if you use the supernatural satan abilities. The more natural ways of death you choose, the more secure the maids and janitors will be with stuff they leave around, and if someone sees you with a screwdriver that you use later to take out a screw in someone´s ladder, the bigger the more careful everyone will be around you, OR they might investigate you. 
You could have used this to your advantage to create branching paths, trying to frame characters for death of other characters, like taking socks of a maid, dipping them in motor oil, hiding them in her room, and then setting a man on fire in that motor oil later. She would have been taken away, and while she is getting incarcerated for murder, you make her lover get drunk and make him jump from the fucking balcony to his death.
Another thing that bothers me is that we get only one murder per chapter. Why in the fucking world couldn´t have had a random chance of someone walking in on us murdering someone, then threatening him to frame the murder on him if they didn´t help us, and dispose of them later?

See? There was so much they could have done, but they didn´t. Instead, they chose a linear open world aproach. Another idea: In the chapter where we kill Gene, there could have been two ways of killing him. Take away Gene´s matches, fill the kitchen with gas, set up the matches behind the doors, and make everyone steer clear of that part of house by distracting everyone on the other side, and while Gene goes to light his cigarette after the distraction event, he fucking explodes that part of the house, which would carry over and affect other parts of the gameplay.

These are just dreams tho. Because I´ve already described this game multiple times: linear semi-open world. There is nothing more to it. 

With that said, do I recommend it? Even after everything I´ve said: yeah, play it. You can find satisfaction if you play this one without help, and if you find some secrets of your own, it´s added bonus. But this is a one and done situation. I finished all of the Lucius games recently.

If you want an interesting story about the son of devil, than play this or the demake version (or both), than Lucius 3.
If you want to be a child serial killer, play Lucius 2.
If you want both, no luck for you.

All of the games have bugs, except Demake, but all of them are something you can use to it.
If you have the patience for that, you will have an unique experience.


About games:

 - Lucius: It is a 3D "point and click"-like game wich focuses on storytelling, gore and wandering around and in the manor. It uses slowmos very badly, even ruined the tense of the last chapter for me. Try to talk to everybody in every chapter for more infos and hints.

 - Lucius demake: First demake I ever played. Much easier to find items. The last chapter is teasing and besides that I like it much better than the original. Also it has the best OST from all of them.

 - Lucius 2: It is now a challenging game, where you have many ways to harvest souls. It is very well made that way (besides bugs of course). In exchange, it has the worst storytelling and character development, but in Lucius 3 they reflected to it very well.

 - Lucius 3: The 3D "point and click"-like gameplay returns with open world and again it´s rather focuses on gore and storytelling. Back to the roots, but better.
 Even it is not a finished game as intended, it´s story is phenomenal. My jaw dropped in front the genuie of the writer(s?).
 It is my favourite from all, because after those mixed stuff the other games gave me, I have finally seen the true Lucius I ever wanted to see.

If I can say that, the first Lucius game is like a movie, the second and demake is like a game and the third is a series that didn´t finished, but closed properly (as possible).

The strongest part of all games are Lucius itself and his strange character development. He never talks (khm...), he just kill poeple, but the small things, like the way he does the murders or how he reacts to certain situations build his style, but you never really know what he really feels or think. That´s his true power, beside being a kid.
In Lucius 3 he is very strong, but he still use that power to outsmart others like in the first game, while in Lucius 2 he is rather aggressive and the gameplay is about that too.


Focus on Lucius itself,
Don´t care about bugs, get used to them,
Have patience to find what you need
And you will have a very great experience you will never forget.

Although this game aged extremely poorly in many aspects, it still is a unique experience which deserves to be played at least once. 

We will play as Lucius, a kid who is the son of the devil. Chapter by chapter we will be tasked by our father with killing people inside the house we live in. 

First it will be staff members, a maid, the butcher, up until more “high profile” targets. The killings must be disguised as accidents, in order to avoid and deflect suspicions about us. 

Every kill will increase our power and eventually we will unlock new abilities, like telekinesis, mind control and fireballs.

The game is really explicit and graphic in depicting the murders, showing exactly how every victim dies with plenty of details. The story is pretty well written too, conveying a nice black humor sort of noir mood.

You play Lucius, a formidable six year-old child. Born on the 6th of June, 1966 (you can do the conversion), Lucius has the honor of being the anti-Christ and all the light-hearted responsibilities that come with it. Visited by his dad on Birthday number six, Lucius is tasked with carrying out the whims of his father: murdering all the inhabitants of Dante Manor.
The game is comprised of nine separate chapters. Each begins with a voice-over and a notebook entry on who your next target is, and concludes with a grisly homicide and a follow-up visit from Satan to grant Lucius new powers and to bolster old ones, such as telekinesis, combustion, and mind-control. While many of the kills are creative, entertaining, and sometimes morbidly funny, what the game often requires of you to reach that moment of satisfaction often results in frustration.
As an anti-hero six-year-old Satan spawn, you’re quite the amalgam of bad-ass and unsuspected hitman – but without much motive or directive. Each kill requires you to piece together sporadic clues to determine what items or tools are necessary to manipulate your target or lure them into places they might not otherwise go (such as face-first into a stove top element to light a cigarette).

The entire game takes place at Dante Manor, an enormous, sprawling estate with dozens of rooms to explore, drawers to rifle through, and objects to steal for your nefarious ends. While the ultimate demise of each target is often original and unpredictable, reaching that moment typically mimics a “Take object A to manipulate object B to get target C to do task D”. As such, there is little freedom in getting to the end result. This is not a sandbox game and does not follow the open-ended format of, for example, the Hitman and Manhunt series – but that difference isn’t necessarily a flaw, as it serves a purpose by bolstering the narrative.
For those who enjoy all aspects of the discovery process, clicking around in different environments and ultimately finding what you’re looking for can be rewarding – although the emotion I frequently experienced was exasperation. With little feedback that you’re on the right course, the game can quickly stop being fun. Because of each mission’s strict requirements, the intended payoffs act more as a relief to pent-up frustration for finally getting it right. There was nothing more disappointing than going into the kitchen and being unable to pick up the butcher knife. The mission requirements are often unclear, as almost the entire mansion is free to roam from murder one. Further, there is no initial tutorial on the sequential nature of your murderous imperatives, so you’ll need to start clicking early, often, and indiscriminately.
Graphically, the game isn’t ugly, but a lot of the colors are washed out, the lighting is unrealistic and interferes with other sources (like the outside light interacting with ambient light), and the animations are jerky. The cutscenes are entertaining but suffer from poor camera placement and direction. Subtracting from the presentation are the unacceptably long load times. This compounds frustration when occasionally you’ll fail a mission because someone may have seen you wielding a screwdriver that you had no business wielding, or overtly using your telekinesis, drawing attention from those around. There are no waypoints, so if you fail, you’re back at the beginning, but first you’ll be staring at a load screen.
The in-game music features some fun, weird, bugle-filled atmospheric tracks, sometimes employing the cellos, violin crescendos, and orchestral choirs that are common of the horror genre. Sadly, the music is often on short loops, and can get annoying or simply feel out of place during parts of the chapters. Speaking about out of place, the game’s voice acting is B-rate at best, suffering at times from a poorly-translated script and inadequate direction. This was especially disappointing due to the game being heavily story-driven and reliant on verbal or conversational cues that felt detached.

Despite the game’s ambitious premise, its many shortfalls overshadow the things it actually does well. The murders are always a treat. Coupled with Lucius’ deadpan death-stare and the ludicrously lavish and ridiculous ways in which targets reach their bloody ends, there is often a sick, dark humor that pervades the game. This is also apparent among the surviving residents and workers as they’re picked off one by one, slowly slipping into depression or insanity, and little Lucius just stands there, taking in all the madness, while still conducting his everyday business of putting away his toys and brushing his teeth (these are sadly further nuisances – chores – that break up the narrative but add to the hilarity).

Lucius is a horror-puzzle game where you play as Lucius, the Antichrist son of Lucifer, and you are tasked with killing everyone in your mansion. I think this game is comparable to the Hitman games, since in both games you have to kill your target silently and creatively. However, while Hitman offers different opportunities and methods to kill your target, in Lucius you must follow very specific steps, so it feels more like a puzzle game than Hitman does. The whole premise of the game is similar to The Omen, a 1976 film featuring Damien, an Antichrist child.

While Agent 47 has many gears to help kill his targets, Lucius has supernatural powers such as telekinesis, mind control, mind wipe, and pyrokinesis. Most of his powers are used to manipulate objects around him that causes the target's death seem like an accident. Pyrokinesis can be used to fight, but it only happens twice in the whole game. There are also "sidequests" in the form of chores, and doing them will give you rewards that can help you. These are not necessary, but there's an achievement for getting all 3 rewards.

The biggest problem of Lucius for me is the darkness, literally. The game applies some kind of dark monotone filter that makes all colors seem dreary. What's worse is when the missions took place in the evening or night. It's literally too dark to see anything, even after raising the gamma and PC brightness. Optimization is also bad, my PC is quite strong but can only run this game in 1280x720 resolution and Medium graphics. Breaking glass objects also causes lag spikes, but easily solved by walking away from that location. 

However Lucius is a pretty okay-ish horror game, so if you like the Hitman games or The Omen happens to be one of your favorite horror movies, don't hesitate to give this game a try. It's quite short and usually goes on a 90% sale, so it's very cheap. I think it would be cooler if Lucius has multiple ways to kill the targets like Hitman, as it increases the replayability.

Lucius is a dark and intriguing horror-adventure game that plunges players into the unsettling world of a young boy with sinister powers and an ominous destiny. Developed by Shiver Games, the game offers a unique twist on the horror genre by placing players in the role of Lucius, a six-year-old child who is, in fact, the son of the devil. This premise sets the stage for a narrative that blends supernatural elements with a disturbing exploration of innocence corrupted, making it a standout title for those who enjoy psychological horror with a strong narrative focus.

The gameplay centers around exploration, puzzle-solving, and stealth as you carry out a series of diabolical tasks within the confines of a sprawling mansion. Lucius’s abilities allow players to manipulate the environment, possess objects, and craft deadly traps, which must be used strategically to eliminate the unsuspecting inhabitants without raising suspicion. The game cleverly encourages creativity, giving you multiple ways to approach each target and experiment with different methods of causing mayhem. This freedom enhances replayability and adds layers of depth to the overall experience, challenging players to think like a sinister child orchestrating chaos from the shadows.

One of the most compelling aspects of Lucius is its atmospheric setting and narrative tone. The game uses its eerie mansion environment to great effect, creating a sense of creeping dread that permeates every corridor and room. The sound design is subtle but effective, with unsettling ambient noises, distant whispers, and haunting music that heighten the tension and contribute to an immersive horror experience. The storyline unfolds through cutscenes and interactions with various characters, slowly revealing the dark family secrets and the boy’s connection to the supernatural forces that drive him. While the pacing can sometimes feel uneven, the narrative remains engaging, especially for players interested in a story-driven horror adventure.

Graphically, Lucius presents a fairly dated but serviceable visual style that suits its eerie atmosphere. The mansion is richly detailed, with a variety of interactive objects that players can use to their advantage. Character models and animations might not be cutting-edge by today’s standards, but they effectively convey the unsettling mood of the game’s world. The design choices emphasize mood and storytelling over flashy graphics, which works in the game’s favor, especially for those who prioritize atmosphere in horror games.

Despite its strengths, Lucius has its flaws. Some players have noted issues with clunky controls and occasional bugs that can disrupt the flow of gameplay. The stealth mechanics, while central to the experience, sometimes feel inconsistent, making it frustrating to avoid detection. Additionally, certain puzzles and objectives can be obscure, requiring trial and error that may test player patience. However, these shortcomings do not overshadow the game’s core appeal, which lies in its unique premise and the dark, immersive world it creates.

In summary, Lucius offers a chilling and unconventional horror adventure that stands out for its perspective and storytelling. Playing as a child of darkness with deadly powers provides a fresh take on the genre, inviting players to explore themes of innocence twisted by evil. While not without technical hiccups and occasional design frustrations, the game’s atmosphere, narrative depth, and creative gameplay mechanics make it a memorable experience for horror enthusiasts looking for something different. Lucius may not be perfect, but it carves out its own niche by delivering a compelling blend of supernatural horror and strategic stealth gameplay that lingers long after the final scene.

Lucius is a great concept, with a well written story and a good voice-actor for the narrator.

The gameplay is very linear, the "pick every object you see and then find out how and where to use them" gameplay. If you explore and pick EVERYTHING right away (when it's not yet needed) you make the game much easier and faster. If you wait until the items are needed before picking them up some parts of the game will become slow and frustrating.

You don't ever leave the house (except for the gardens). There's only one way to execute every kill, and you have to find out what it is (no physics involved like in HITMAN). Also, when the game progresses you unlock new skills, but you can't use them unless you are meant to for that specific kill (you can't go around burning people with your fireball skill). So the feeling you get is as if the story was already written and you only had to recreate exactly what had happened, instead of making your own story.

Conclusion: Good concept, execution could be better, but still fun (mostly). Buy if it's on sale.

Lucius was a ball of fun and frustration all at the same time. I went into Lucius thinking that it was going to be an absolutely terrifying game, but it was more humorous than anything. There were some parts that were a little too much and just had me thinking "whoa" after a cutscene. But, for the most part, it was pretty fun to run around a huge ass mansion wreaking havoc as a satanic child. The puzzles were pretty difficult for me to figure out most of the time, so Google will be your friend if you're ever stuck. But have fun exploring and trying to figure out the riddles/puzzles yourself first before googling!

If you're someone who is looking for an easy game to 100%, Lucius might be for you. It's relatively easy, and I was about 80% done with the achievements from just one casual playthrough. You're able to reload certain chapters if you missed something small, so you don't have to do an entire fresh playthrough just to get certain achievements-- which I found really convenient. The only achievement that's "hard" to get is playing Lucius for 40 hours. You can just leave the game running, but it can't be during the last chapter, as for some reason, it won't count towards the achievement. So, just load up one of the earlier chapters and leave your game running. :)

If you're looking for a great 100% achievement walkthrough/guide for Lucius, I used this one by JJblackNight: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1648205461

All in all, this game is pretty fun, but like I said previously, it has its frustrating moments-- it [b]is[/b] a game from 2014. Definitely get it on sale or as is!

It was late 2018; mid to late November when I first launched this game. I had taken the day off work as I had awoken feeling unwell. If I recall correctly, I was experiencing mild head congestion and perhaps a sniffled nose. It was a cold, cloudy morning, trees scarce from the leaves that had long abandoned their home, unlike me who at this time had still lived at my mothers house. What was usually a loud and busy household was instead replaced with a quiet and calm environment on account of everyone at work. 

I had purchased this game months before but hadn't gotten around to playing it yet. With it being around 7:30-8:00 am, my usual online acquaintances were asleep and unavailable. I briefly checked the online games I play casually to see if there were any populated servers, but I had no such luck. 

Sitting there with the day ahead of me I began mindlessly scrolling through my Games Library, when I saw this game not yet installed. I went over to the Store Catalog and searched it up to remind myself of what kind of game this was. 
After viewing the trailers, to say I was enticed would be an understatement. 

I enthusiastically clicked on the install button and fixed myself a warm cup of coffee. Back at my mothers she did not use a traditional coffee maker, but rather a Tassimo single cup coffee. I was never fond of the coffee or the brands my mother preferred, but this was my best option. After adding one small teaspoon of sugar and a generous splash of milk, I briskly stirred my coffee and headed back to my bedroom. 

The installation was complete and I quickly immersed myself in the story. Playing the character Lucius was quite enjoyable; devious tricks and plans to sabotage peoples lives and being able to kill them in creative ways was truly exciting. I admire the developers creativity and their ability to execute the deaths so well. I found the story rich for the characters and I was impressed with the amount of details that went into each of them, as well as into the environment. There was a lot of depth in the characters as well as the objectives. I'm not the most intelligent Gamer™, and found some tasks too tricky, but luckily I had google on my side to help me execute these murders. 

During my gameplay experience I took a brief intermission in the early afternoon to try something I hadn't ever before: Skip The Dishes. Now, I'm familiar with ordering delivery Chinese or pizza over the phone, and even online, but the idea of having a stranger not affiliated with the franchise bringing me my food, independently of the store? It was a bit unnerving, but I was hungry and determined to obtain Wendy's sweet sweet Chili. The ordering and delivery went better than expected, and I excitedly ate my chili while continuing with the game, which also was still easy and enjoyable. 

I found the ending to this game very rewarding, and I anticipate on purchasing the 2nd and 3rd game for Lucius. I hope this review helped and I truly could not recommend this game enough.

После дискотеки мы с сестрой возвращались домой. И по дороге поссорились достаточно сильно. Она развернулась и пошла к другу, ну а я продолжила свою дорогу домой. Пришла, зашла в маленький домик (у нас их два — один большой, в котором живут постоянно, другой маленький, который открывают только на лето). В этом маленьком домике нас с сестрой поселили, то есть мы в нем были одни.

Разделась, легла на кровать, лежу и думаю о чем-то своем. Вдруг в прихожей раздались шаги — тяжелые такие. Я подумала, что это сестра моя вернулась. Отвернулась к стенке и лежу дальше. Открылась дверь, кто-то прошел и лег ко мне на кровать. Я лежу, не поворачиваюсь — так обиделась на сестру. И вдруг под окном раздается голос: «Светлана (это я), открой мне дверь, это сестра твоя — извини, если обидела!».

Вот тут у меня волосы дыбом встали. Я лежу, шелохнуться не могу и думаю: «Кто лежит со мной?». Начинаю медленно поворачиваться и вижу два желтых глаза и смутную темную фигуру. Who is lying next to me?

In the summer, my parents and I went to a village. It's located not far from Yoshkar-Ola. Well, of course, since it's summer, that means discos and hanging out until morning. This story happened on the third day after arriving at the country house.

After the disco, my sister and I were walking home. And on the way, we had a pretty serious argument. She turned around and went to a friend's place, well, and I continued on my way home. I arrived, went into the small house (we have two of them — one big one, where people live permanently, and another small one, which is only opened in the summer). My sister and I were settled in this small house, meaning we were the only ones in it.

I got undressed, lay down on the bed, and was just lying there thinking my own thoughts. Suddenly, footsteps sounded in the hallway — heavy ones, like that. I thought it was my sister coming back. I turned towards the wall and kept lying there. The door opened, someone came in and lay down on the bed with me. I'm lying there, not turning around — I was so mad at my sister. And then suddenly, a voice comes from under the window: "Svetlana (that's me), open the door for me, it's your sister — sorry if I offended you!"

That's when my hair stood on end. I'm lying there, unable to move, and thinking: "Who is lying with me?" I start to slowly turn around and see two yellow eyes and a vague dark figure. As soon as I saw it, I jumped up and ran out of the house like a bat out of hell. My sister says: "What's wrong with you? Your face looks so..." I told her everything immediately. She didn't believe me at first, but then she remembered the look on my face again and fell silent...

Overall? I do recommend this game, pretty cool experience but do be aware of its age.

"Lucius" is a bizarre game. It's a third-person point-and-click murder mystery with a B-movie attitude toward the plot. Depending on what you expect from the game, it can either be awesome or a letdown.

Even after completing "Lucius" twice, I am not sure how the game wants to be perceived. It has a serious tone, but the things it delivers are absurd. In one scene, for example, a broken ceiling fan DECAPITATES a man! No, there is no rationalization offered; it just so happened that a regular ceiling fan, hanging and swinging on a wire, was able to cut someone's head clean off. The only thing missing was a cheesy one-liner from Lucius, like: "Be careful with fans—they can make you lose your head!" Instead, the tone was gloomy. Murder scenes are gruesome and grim, as much as their absurdity allows. This mismatch between the tone and what happens on the screen may be confusing, but once accepted, it can become comedic. It then starts to feel as if "Lucius" tells a joke with a straight face. A darkly humorous joke

The gameplay loop is simple: identify a victim, spot an opportunity for an accident or a sneaky murder, find and apply items to initiate it, maybe use superpowers, and enjoy a murder cutscene. Repeat for about 7 hours. Everything is heavily scripted, so there is no room for creativity. Some say it gets boring quickly, but as for me, I've enjoyed the game till the end. Not so much for the gameplay as for the sheer curiosity of how the story will unfold and what wacky ways of murder are there.

Most of the game is spent running around and searching for items in Dante Manor. The manor is spacious and can feel like a labyrinth at first. Although it's easy to get lost, its layout is logical and believable. It takes time to get used to, but that's due to how huge the manor is. Other than that, the manor is detailed and good-looking. I enjoyed walking around and looking at it. At one point, I was able to memorize its layout and navigate with no problems.

The manor is populated by the Wagner family and their servants. The main character is an antichrist, a devil's son, who is tasked with sacrificing the souls of the residents of Dante's Manor. In return, he is promised supernatural powers. And so Lucius, the titular protagonist, sets off on his murderous journey to kill one person a month until there is no one left. Inhabitants, or victims, have flat personalities and linear routines they follow unless it is their turn to be sacrificed. The simplicity of characters is both good and bad. "Good" because there is no sympathy for victims and you can enjoy murdering them without guilt. This point does not become apparent until Lucius decides to kill the old butler, who gives the impression of being the nicest man in the world. Killing him in a horrific freak accident was genuinely heartbreaking. But it's also "bad" for the same reason. The fact of murder has no bearing. Nobody seems to react to what happened to their friends and colleagues. Everyone just carries on normally. Only Lucius' mother and "so-called" father seem to freak out. It would have been so much more impactful to see how the household descends into paranoia, chaos, and despair. It would be cool to see character routines and dialogue change to show mental breakdowns. For example, creating moments where they cry, drown sorrow in booze, or reassure each other that "everything is going to be okay." It would make characters more human. Killing them would be much harder, and the fact that you are doing horrific things would be more apparent. It also would make the ludicrous ways they die so much more comedic. There is a big emotional difference between "an NPC gets killed by a player" and "a God-loving nun gets her head crushed with a piano by a six-year-old antichrist."

Gameplay-wise, "Lucius" is very similar to point-and-click adventure games: find items and apply them in a specific order. The difference is that "Lucius" has a free-roaming third-person perspective. It makes navigation around locations much smoother, but does not exclude pixel hunting. In fact, "Lucius" modifies "pixel hunting" into "prop hunting" due to the game not always being clear which exact object it requires. For example, there is a moment where a character asks for a specific bottle of wine. The character himself sits right next to at least three wine racks. None of the wines from them seem to satisfy him. Every other bottle in the house does not either. The solution is to go to a wine cellar, look at the wine racks’ year numbers, and then prop-hunt the only interactive bottle at the top of a rack. At first it might even be unknown that the mansion has a wine cellar! To deduce that "the bottle of "30's wine" is there would be another leap of thought. To somehow spot the only interactive bottle at the very top of a rack is ludicrous. "Lucius" has many moments where you can get stuck because the game requires a very specific action or item. This can be mitigated to an extent by going around the mansion and collecting everything that you can. Nearly every item is available from the start. It makes it much easier, since you can look into the inventory and see what object could perform the required task instead of running around and guessing. So, run around Dante Mansion and explore! Don’t be creative in a heavily scripted game; find specific items to solve specific actions. Sometimes, to complete murder sequence initiation, Lucius has to use his devilish super-powers, such as telekinesis, mind-control, or a fire ball. If these sound cool, they will not be after "Lucius." The "superpowers," like items, can only be used in specific situations. Pretty much like in a point-and-click adventure game.

Although the past paragraph painted a negative picture of "Lucius’" gameplay, the gameplay itself is not just bad. It shares the flaws of point-and-click adventure games, but it also shares what makes them good. Each murder is a little puzzle. The reward for solving a puzzle is a gruesome freak accident cutscene. If you enjoy point-and-click adventures or are a fan of "Final Destination" movies, you might enjoy Lucius as well.


All in all, it’s okay. "Okay" is the most suitable word to describe my opinion of "Lucius." It's bizarre, but not outstanding. Can be used to kill some time and innocent people. If you expect Hitman-like gameplay or a serious, engaging story, you will be disappointed. If you are open-minded to an odd point-and-click adventure experience, you might enjoy causing mischief in Dante Manor.

If you're intrigued by this game's aesthetic and the idea of being a cute little boy that secretly murders people with the help of your demon daddy, then you will probably enjoy this game. If you go into this game expecting something like Hitman, just know that it's not [i]really[/i] like that.

[u][b]Okay, so what [i]is[/i] the game like?[/b][/u]
At its core, Lucius is more like a puzzle game in the sense that you must find and use objects in the correct way in order to complete the murder and progress the story. There is generally only one solution to each chapter, but the game is charming nonetheless. You know those point and click adventures where you have to combine and use objects in your inventory in the right locations at the right time? It's sort of like that, but in 3D.

[u][b]The cons(?)[/b][/u]
The game can be a little odd or buggy at times (I never encountered anything game breaking though), it can be easy to get lost in the mansion (especially when the doors automatically close behind you), the stealth segments are a little annoying, and some of the executions or story beats come across as rather goofy (though I'd argue this is part of the charm-- much like horror movies).

[u][b]To get the most enjoyment out of this game...[/b][/u]
I recommend taking your time when you play this game for the first time, because if you use a walkthrough then you may find it goes by way too fast; once you've memorized all the 'puzzles,' it's very easy to speed through this game without actually taking in any of it. The hints in the journal are usually pretty straightforward, so I'd use guides sparingly until you've already beaten the game once and are now trying to 100% it.

If you [i]are[/i] someone who likes to 100% games, Lucius isn't that bad, though some of the achievements feel really out of place. For example, the achievement to[spoiler]burn people alive five times[/spoiler]requires you to redo the same chapter over a couple times since this doesn't happen naturally in a playthrough for some reason, but it's still pretty easy. There's also some really tedious ones like to play for 40 hours when this game is pretty linear and takes nowhere near that amount of time to beat. Just leave the game on in the background for this one; it's pretty dumb, but it's entirely based on your Steam playtime (count yourself lucky because it used to not be). I also 100%d the game myself (as you can most likely tell from my 40 hour playtime) and it wasn't very difficult, so if you're an achievement hunter like me, you may or may not find it satisfying in that regard. 

[u][b]TL;DR![/b][/u]
In conclusion, the game is a little goofy and surprisingly linear, but I still found it to be very charming and pretty enjoyable to play through. If you go into this game expecting an absolute masterpiece of gameplay, you will likely be disappointed. The game is fun because of the charming characters, simple story (for now), and there's just something hilarious about riding around on your tricycle as a little rich kid living in a huge mansion, and then murdering all its inhabitants one by one on the low. The game genuinely holds my attention because I just can't wait to see who the next victim will be and what creative way Lucius will find to kill them.

If that sounds appealing to you, go for it! The game isn't that expensive anyway, and it's an even better deal if you can snag it on sale.

A daunting game start to finish. Although I bought all three games in the franchise, I can't say that the sequel made as big of an impression to me as the first game.

In this franchise, you are the devil's son, and like the devil's son you will act, wrecking havoc and creating despair within the manor in which you reside. The kills feel like they have weight to them; people will react, fear will rise, and unlike the sequel (haven't gotten around to Lucius 3, so can't comment on that one yet) your actions will have consequences. The story is fitting for a game of this caliber, nothing too extreme.

The music is chilling, but never too in-your-face. I've read somewhere that the game's graphics designer produced some of my personal favourite tracks for no extra cost (e.g. Devil's Fairground) because the team was running short on budget, but needed more music, which I find really really cool and creative of them. 

The animations and controls are Lucius' weaker points. This game attempts to touch on taboo topics in cold and unforgiving ways, but oftentimes fails to visualise it properly because of the weird lighting, choppy animations, or outright goofy bugs happening quite often during gameplay. But even still, I wouldn't say that those are reasons not to try the game if you're interested.

Overall the first game definitely has a story to tell, and is certainly worth trying out. The atmosphere can reel the player in right from the start, I found myself binging this game up until late at night to figure out what the next step is gonna be, or how the story and characters will unfold next.

I wish the sequel carried this energy or expanded on it. Amazing work to the team!

Lucius is a very interesting game about a 10 year old going on a rampage in his family home. Granted, to actually go on said rampage, you'll need to follow a steam guide (I recommend this one right here: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=182953522) as there is only one way of killing each target and if you struggle with common sense like I did, you'll need it. Trust me, since the game doesn't really give any hints as to who or how your going to pull off each murder.

The game has you scheme to kill each of the human subjects (mother, maid you name it), spread over 18 chapters, as you progress unlocking Lucius' powers: Telekinesis, mind control, combustion and memory erase given to him by the devil. As well as doing side tasks like cleaning lucius' room, taking out the rubbish, grabbing a buttler a bottle of 1930s champagne and collecting dirty washing for you to sort into seprate baskets, you'll also be collecting Items and weapons that will come in handy for future chapters. 

(If you're an achievement hunter, there are a few housekeeping ones that need you to repeat an action/task multiple times to unlock like: opening cupboards, smashing/dropping items, turning on and off TVs and using Lucius' abilities as you unlock them)

After a while, it does get repetitive, so I would come back to it on and off if you get bored easily. 

Graphically it was OK. I was playing this on a Steam Deck at medium settings, so I know the game is capable of more on better hardware. 

My only main issue with Lucius was the control scheme. On Steam Deck, the game wasn't responding properly with the set buttons, so I had to find a useable layout on Steam Input and then edit it to what I liked as I started the game. It might be helpful if you plan to play on a controller or steam deck. Search for "Playable control scheme for steam deck - Lucius" on the steam input page (It's not perfect but it gets the job done) 

Overall, since I got this game on sale, I would say it was worth it. Mainly because of all the different ways Lucius kills each victim, and although the game's narrative feels uncoincidental to justify each killing, if you haven't played narrative based games in awhile (like me) it's a good game to get started with.

Lucius is an older title that still holds up surprisingly well today. Despite its age, the graphics and game physics remain impressive, capturing a chilling 1970s atmosphere that adds a distinct charm to its unsettling narrative. The dimly lit halls of Dante Manor, eerie background music, and vintage aesthetics all contribute to a timeless horror experience that continues to engage players years after its release.

What really sets Lucius apart is its unique concept. Instead of running from monsters, you are the threat—playing as Lucius, the devil’s son, orchestrating deaths in a Final Destination-style fashion using tricks or powers granted to you. The game’s dark, puzzle-based approach to murder is both disturbing and inventive, requiring strategy and patience rather than brute force.

While it does have occasional bugs and some dated animations, they never truly detract from the overall experience. In fact, they’ve become part of the game’s charm over time. The voice acting and storytelling, combined with its sinister tone and clever design, make Lucius a cult classic well worth revisiting.

The biggest problem with this game is its linearity. Each death is planned in advance and it is impossible to kill a person in several ways. There is one thing the creators have defined and there is absolutely nothing we can do about it. Of course, every subsequent elimination is to some extent fun, but the possibility to kill a person in several different ways would be great.

Travelling through successive rooms of the great mansion becomes boring over time, when after a few dozen minutes we know exactly every nook and cranny in every room. Although the mansion seems big, it is quite the opposite. It is known that it would be pointless to allow people to leave the house, but the creators could introduce more space.

[h1]Summary[/h1]

I'd like to give this game a high rating, because I even had fun in it, but the game has its disadvantages, which may discourage many players from buying it, making it less attractive. Generally I recommend if you want to buy this game and go through it once. In total, the game takes about 6 hours and the price is adequate to the quality.

Lucius is a psychological horror stealth game that puts you in the shoes of a 6-year-old boy who is the son of Lucifer. You have to use your telekinesis and mind control powers to kill the members of your household in a series of deadly accidents. The game is set in a gothic mansion, where you have to explore, find clues, and avoid suspicion.

The game has a full narrative, narrated by Chris Parnell, who adds a dark-humorous tone to the game. Игра также известна своими интересными головоломками, которые требуют сообразительности и логического мышления. Разнообразие этих головоломок заставляет игрока постоянно придумывать новые стратегии и решать трудности, что добавляет дополнительного остроумия и увлекательности в игровой процесс.

Важным аспектом "Lucius" является захватывающий сюжет, который привлекает внимание и не отпускает до самого конца. Фасад идеальной семьи, скрытые тайны и шокирующие открытия создают атмосферу загадки и непредсказуемости, что поддерживает стимуляцию интереса и желание узнать, как развиваются события.

Игра дополняется возможностью кататься на велосипеде, что добавляет разнообразия в игровой процесс. Это позволяет не только передвигаться по игровому миру быстрее и эффективнее, но и встречать новые интересные места и открывать дополнительные возможности.

Наконец, "Lucius" радует приятной звуковой составляющей. Звуки окружающего мира, музыка и голосовое сопровождение удачно подчеркивают атмосферу игры, создавая более полное и погружающее впечатление.

В целом, "Lucius" станет настоящим увлечением для поклонников жанра, предлагая хорошую оптимизацию, множество жестокости, интересные головоломки, захватывающий сюжет, возможность кататься на велосипеде и приятную звуковую составляющую. Эта игра не оставит равнодушным ни одного игрока.

This game was a pleasant surprise to me since I've seen this game spring up a few times around Youtube, I remember Pewdiepie playing this back in the day and my expectations weren't anything to great since I realised how old the game is. 

My surprise was how much I actually enjoyed this game, it was a nice breathe of fresh air since I have never seen a game like this with the challenges and puzzles you conquer to slowly killing people in creative ways. You take on the role of Lucius which is the son of Lucifer aka the name for the devil. The motives of the game are simple, eliminating the family and members of the household using the powers you slowly unlock throughout the progress like telekinesis and mind control to set up accidental deaths and even framing members of the house. 

The graphics are average for the time of writing this but I still need to play the other games in the series to see the advancements but this wouldn't have an effect since the game for the time would've been impressive. The game suffers depth since there isn't a whole lot of gameplay elements since each chapter sets up a scenario that you are stuck by. The game is definitely something different to try but having two achievements that make you play for 20 and 40 hours when the game is only around 8/10 hours long, it's a bit silly since like I previously mentioned, the game is limited to the chapters and them orchestrated murders. 

The game itself is very clever on how you perform these murders but however, the game's biggest problem for me is the lack of guidance the player is given for each day since it starts of pretty self explanatory but then slowly slips and you are given very little information besides the tips since leaving core aspects of a video game not explained well enough. 

The voice acting is laughable and the characters behaviour is very much poorly designed but again, I'll let it slide for the 2012 release and I have played worse games, the element I give this a positive review is that I have never played something quite like this, I look forward to playing the series. 

The game is also riddled with bugs, becoming stuck on the stairs in the courtyard, clipping through the wall on the left wing stairs down to the corridor, AI walking into walls and being spotted when behind solid walls. Also, a poor design of the tricycle is that the hands of Lucius are no where near the handlebars and also with animations like filling up the water bottle, there is little effort to making this look more realistic. 

To conclude, the game is old pretty much and therefore you have to cut it some slack, I know I have more negatives but just the fact the game is different to fps games or strategies is why I would recommend it to try, I won't confirm you'll have an enjoyable experience but it's fun.

In the briefest possible sentiment, my feelings for Lucius are mixed. With clear thematic inspiration from the Omen, Lucius offers a fresh foray into horror by giving you control over the demonically-influenced child, Lucius. You're directed to kill the staff of your parents' estate, and it isn't your lot to question why. Lucifer himself appears in a dissapointingly trite manner: an obliquely evil man in a suit, grinning maniacally. Preferable to depictions of a man in a red leotard and a trident, he still fails to convey a palpable sense of dreadful terror or villainy. 
 Blessed (or cursed?) with unholy powers, some light puzzle solving is required to kill the servants in seemingly-accidental and  gorey fashion. The staff aren't exactly likeable, so there's no sense you're doing any real harm to innocents. One could even argue that the devil is being quite helpful by terminating unsavoury workers. Lucius never does any of the murdering directly; rather, he manipulates the environment into creatively lethal traps. These traps are clever, and the ensuing death scenes are appropriately violent.
  Dissapoinment stems from three areas: the cheesiness, the impotent morality, and the wasted oppurtunity. The most obvious failure lies in the seemingly deliberate nature of the game's campy vibe. The narration provided by the investigating officer would fit perfectly into a b-movie horror romp. No one's reactions to the freak-accident murders carry any sense of gravity. Lucifer himself is better suited for a cartoon villain than a manipulative murderer. The tone isn't ominous, oppressive, or morally horrifying- all qualities it *should* be. Think about it: you play as a child who is being directly influenced by Satan to kill innocent people in unspeakable ways as part of a grander purpose known only to the devil himself. This subversion of moral principle- that children are innocent- should lead the player into feeling they're proceeding into the blasphemous; which ties into my second point.
  Feeling is subjective, but if the game is trying to make you feel as if you're really controlling a murderous child, it fails. Instead, you feel as if you're zipping around and doing Myst-lite style puzzles to knowck off a few annoying charicatures. There' sno sense of innocence lost, since Lucius is devoid of any character, and the game isn't scary. The buildup to the kills is monotonous, with gathering items and some stealth-lite gameplay. You don't feel that there are real-world consequences to the deaths, as neither your parents nor the other staff are seriously disturbed or upset. There's no repurcussions, no mourning, and no shocking cruelty about it. Contrast this with one of my favorite morally torturous moments in gaming from the Amnesia DLC *minor spoiler*: You are forced to kill an NPC that's strapped down to a table to progress. His pleas for help inspire guilt, and you feel horror at what you choose to do. There are similar moments in SOMA.
  One should feel that, as Lucius, they're doing something abominable. A child killing innocent people is something inherently abhorrent, and yet Lucius fails to provide that.
 Ultimately, Lucius is an example of wasted potential. Evil protagonists, when done right, make the player feel guilt vicariously, and from that guilt a sense of dread develops. Or an angle where there's sadistic pleasure would have also been welcome, as you take a sick joy from doing what you're told. Lucius should be praised for seeking to do something not already hashed and rehashed a million times. It avoids tropes like the Insane Asylum, Hospital, or Zombies. It does not, however, avoid being totally unfrightening or monotonous. 
  I want to like Lucius, and I'm not strongly negative towards the game. I don't, however, recommend it to anyone save the truly dedicated fans of indie horror. Lucius isn't a bad game, only sadly mediocre.

Lucius is one of those games that has a very interesting idea, but executes it horribly. This game sounded like it was going to be waaay more fun then it turned out to be. 

I can't say much about Lucius, because as you can see I only have about an hour of playtime on record. I didn't choose to only play an hour, the game is just so buggy that I couldn't manage to get any farther. Half of the time I can't play because it glitches so much. 

On top of all that, the whole game is very linear. The entire gameplay consist of finding the item you are supposed to find and then using it on the objective. (ex: find screwdriver click stove, wait. Find lock, click freezer, wait.) There are no paths to branch onto, and no choices the come with the game. You have to do what the game wants you to do, and you have no free will to decide yourself. The most side missions you can do is to do your chores for money.That usually involves picking up blocks and putting them in a chest.

Even the powers in Lucius cannot be used freely. Towards the beginning of the game you are granted different powers. Sounds cool right? Not really... You are told when to use that power and you can't use it any other time then when you are prompted to. With how buggy the game is too, the powers can be a hassle to use. 

Another problem with Lucius is the voice acting. It's... pretty bad. Also Lucius himself lacks character. He doesn't show emotion, change his facial expression, say anything, or do anything to show that he is a character. Sure, he is possessed, but that's no excuse. I'd rather him do a cheesy evil grin then be a walking cardboard that is there to do one objective to the next. 

I may have only stated negative things about Lucius this whole review, but I will say that it could be worth it if hugely discounted or in a cheap bundle. The story can be somewhat interesting and the deaths are great to watch for the sadistic side that we all have. It's not a horrible game, but it's definitely not worth the $10 price tag. Especially with how buggy it can be. I say pick Lucius up on sale ONLY if you like very linear storytelling. Oh, and also pull up a walkthrough because the game is almost impossible to figure out without one.

The chores can be quite tedius and at times, similarly to the main objectives, it can be impossibly difficult to figure out what to do.  I was given a chore as simple as "take out the trash" but no further hints were given. The game lacks mouse control in the inventory menu which makes navigation through the most utilized menu feel awkward and clunky, no idea how that happened when the game was only released on PC.

Overall, this game did not capture my attention like I thought it would -- initially giving me hitman vibes, I came in very hopeful for an open, "do the objective however you'd like", kind of game.  As a result, I can only recommend this game on sale if you're feeling particularly curious.

I really anticipated this game ever since it was first announced. I waited for it to be released. And then it did, and the reviews were not kind. I thought I will still like it, until I started the game. 19 minutes later I wrote this review.

It was the most boring opening I have ever seen. The background music was the most uninspired I have ever heard. The voice acting was jarring at best. Stiff and emotionless. The writing lies somewhere between banal and cliche, at times unapologetically indifferent, or unapologetically dumbass, for the lack of a better word. A woman died and the police concluded it was heart attack, and the detective who just arrived concurred, stating that it was typical of women her age, before he even set foot into the house. That was all I could take before I shut down the game.

Controls were unintuitive. Explanations were a mystery in itself. I spent 3 minutes trying to figure out how to use a lock when you don't have a way to select it even when you see it on screen. In the previous step, the game told you to pick it up, then it instructed you to 'holster' it. Then the game asked you to use it, without explaining that you need to 'unholster' it before you can use it. Brilliant. 

In the 19 minutes that I have played the game, I have probably played it for 5 minutes. I spent the other 14 waiting for the game to load, watching slow moving cutscenes that tells you what you already know, listening to words that hardly inspires, instill fear, or peak my interest in any way. It was more interesting watching paint dry.

Also, instead of opting for a first person perspective, the developers wanted to replicate a movie feel and go third person instead. I know, they are trying to recreate the tricycle scene of The Shinning, but ever wondered how awkward it is to control someone in-game like that? And that's not to mention how they always have to center the camera looking directly at Lucius, who admittedly looked creepy in the game. It's a wonder then, how no one suspected him.

Do I recommend this game? No. Will I continue to play it till the end? No. Will I buy Lucius II? No. Should you play this game? Depends. If you are patient and don't care about quality as much, you may enjoy it. If you are critical like I am, you will balk at the notion that this game was even made.

Lucius is a 3D puzzle/adventure game where you control a young child who murders various people around you.   The developer relies on the shock value to push sales.    

While the gameplay may be acceptable, the game has a couple of flaws which render it unacceptable.  Firstly, a bug prevents the mouse pointer from displaying in the inventory screen which makes inventory operations impossible, but this is required to progress the game.  Secondly, there's limited graphics support and no support for anything over 1080p, which is disappointing and doesn't meet modern standards.

Basically, it's The Omen movies meets the Hitman games. Unfortunately, the concept and the style are NOT enough to make Lucius work.

You play as a demonic child tasked by the Devil himself with murdering various people in the large manor home where you live. You have supernatural powers and a true thirst for blood as you make the kills.

The game looks decent for its age but this is clearly NOT a AAA title so don't expect to be wowed by the visuals.

Like the earlier Hitman games, it suffers from being too vague. It's often hard to know exactly what you need to do. You often run around this huge home unsure of where to go next or what items you need. I know some of the more recent Hitman games hold your hand a little too much but Hitman: Absolution got the balance right. Being vague would be okay but Lucius seems to want you to kill in a very specific way without all the possibilities offered in Hitman. Maybe Lucius offers more later on but I just found it too frustrating in the early chapters and was resorting to looking at a guide. Using a guide kind of renders the game pointless as the challenge comes entirely from merely figuring out what the hell you need to do. Again, sorry to keep going back to Hitman but they at least provide a challenge with actually executing your kill rather than just working out what to do. It also means games such as Hitman provide more replay value as you can kill your target in different ways.

The controls in Lucius are okay; I didn't really have any issues in that department.

I really was impressed by the style of this game. The opening level where you kill a woman in a freezer and then meet Satan was terrific. Unfortunately, the developers have just made this too much of a tedious puzzle rather than a challenging stealth game. I just feel the makers of games such as Hitman, Splinter Cell and even Assassins Creed would have done a much better job with the gameplay.

This is one of the worst games I have ever played. If you like context dependent "find the magic pixel" games wearing the disguise of a puzzle/stealth game then this is perfect for you. WHO WAS THIS MADE FOR? Omen fans? Were people really clamoring for shitty controls and contrived plots? How about broken stealth segments that rely on repetition with little to no indication of where enemies are? I can not emphasise enough how terrible this game is.
 You play Lucius, the antichrist born through the machinations of your grandfather who made a pact with the devil to gain power and money. Now you have to go through a mansion and kill people as offerings to Satan in an effort to increase your power. This is done by finding little items hidden throughout the one location in the game and using them to engineer traps or situations that you can influence through your satanic powers that end with someone dying. I guess it's a good game for... snuff enthusists? The payoff to solving the puzzles is a gruesome cutscene sometimes followed by a new power to use that are highly sensitive to context. There's no experimentation, no alternate paths, just a set puzzle with one often obscure conclusion. God help you if you don't know where to get an item that you need to solve a puzzle. It'll usually be tucked away, some colorless chunk on the washed-out palate that you need to click on. Speaking of items, there's an inventory where you store particular items that relate to the story but there's no differentiation between the items you can pick up and the junk that is strewn throughout the house that you can just pick up and HOLD. Sometimes you'll even need to just pick up the items you can't put in your inventory! The house, which is the only setting, is featureless and huge. You can run around up and down stairs, but if you turn a corner too fast or make some minute adjustment with the camera you're going to get lost. Every room and every hallway looks the same, but after about 4 hours of playing I stopped having to refer to the map every 10 seconds.
 The characters are all terribly stiff archetypes capering around and delivering lines through terrible voice acting. Not many lines were recorded, so expect to hear repeated dialogue a LOT. Another part of the story is told through what seems to be the diary entries of a detective named "McGuffin" (hilarious) but I have NO IDEA why these segments were included. Who cares about what some detective is doing when that isn't the focus of the game at all? Why make that a thing? There's no mystery being solved for the player. You know EXACTLY what's happening because the 10 minute intro sequence spelled everything out for you. No tension is built through this parallel exposition and no new information is gained. It just turns into a boring sequence of people jabbering at each other, faking emotion while delivering tired and predictable lines that usually pan out like this:
"I'm a detective who can't figure out why people keep killing themselves."
"Something weird is going on and the my upcoming election can't handle the scandal if the public gets wind of all these people killing themselves in my home."
"I know. It's so WEIRD though."
Now repeat that between every one of the 18 chapters.

It has a nice concept, but ultimately the game is just very poorly executed. On the technical side I've experienced numerous glitches and a few crashes. In-game the inventory and 'mission log' are very awkward to use, and the map is broken. The game offers little support for your objectives. As it has some puzzle elements this isn't necessarily a bad thing, but the game has such tight grip on how a specific objective or 'kill' has to be executed that some kind of support would be nice. The fact that the game's kills are largely scripted doesn't even bother me that much. The main frustration lies in the fact that you have to carry it out exactly as the game wants you to. For instance, halfway through the game you are tasked with carrying water outside without gaining any suspicion. As all but one character are in the same room this could have been as easy as taking a bucket from the laundry room, filling it with water and carrying it outside without bumping into any NPC. Instead, the game wants you to go to a very specific room and take a very specific object to carry the water around. Unfortunately it doesn't end there. Some of the more interesting sections have you sneaking through the mansion at night. As some of the NPCs are still awake you have to take care not to bump into them. However, as the game is rather unforgiving in this, such sequences quickly turn into trial and error. In the game, you use specific powers such as telekinesis and mind control to achieve objectives. A downside is that simple things like picking up stuff or opening doors are treated in the same manner, meaning that this form of interaction also has to be selected from a hotkey. This became frustrating when I spent five minutes trying to open a door but wasn't able to do so as I still had telekinesis selected as active ability. When using a power such as telekinesis or mind control you have to aim extremely careful for it to take effect. Towards the end, this became so tricky that I had to go to the options menu to considerably lower my mouse sensitivity. The game has some annoying invisible walls (or rather 'fences') placed around some objects which obscure your ability to toss fireballs past them. A plus side is that this is one of the very few games where you play a true villain (not just an antihero) and that the atmosphere is very nice. It is just pitiful that the game is so poorly executed.

Tl;dr: nice concept; bad execution.

If you like puzzle games with smooth controls and a refined stealth system, then this is definitely [i]NOT[/i] the game for you. 

I can't think of a kind word to say about Lucien, either the titular character or his "adventure". The entire thing is on rails, to the point of explaining what happens before you do it — no suspense, not even the illusion of choice — and constantly swapping between flagrant handholding and dropping you into a room with no idea what to do except flail at the glitchy and painfully-limited interface until something happens. 

Then there's the horrible model animation; characters's limbs and held objects routinely clip through things, and it doesn't seem like they bothered at all to syncronise movements to interactions.. Despite there being very few interactions to be displayed. The ONLY positive is the well-detailled house itself, but you'd better get used to it because you never go anywhere [i]else[/i].

All in all, Lucius takes the worst from point-and-click games and combines it with the worst from 3d RPGs.. and I haven't even mentioned the part where the [i]six year old child[/i] you play takes photographs of people having sex, or visits a room full of nothing but softcore pornography and sex toys. One has to wonder whether this game was made for anything other than shock value.

I really want to like this game. I want to like it so much that I played through the whole thing, despite realizing how bad it was going to be 20 minutes in. It's right up my alley with its grizley subject matter and over-the top style. Everything is lovably purple, with the number 666 showing up pretty much anywhere any kind of number is called for. On that level the game is brilliant. 

But aside from a lovable style, there's not actually much of a game here. There's no freedom, no challenge. Each level drops you into the house, where you follow a line on a map until you run into a certain NPC. The game shouts "There! That's the person you're trying to kill on this level!" Then you check your notebook for some hint at how the game wants you to get that job done. You follow that hint until you reach another hint, then follow that hint, and so on, until someone dies. There's never more than a single path towards killing any given target, so there's no decisions to be made. The only thing that might actually be considered a challenge is figuring out what the hints mean. The hints oscilate between so obvious as to be trivial, and so obtuse as to be useless. There's no happy middle between the two. No sense of satisfaction in figuring stuff out.  

Then there are the times when you need a tool that isn't already in your inventory. Some specific item, like a screwdriver. Your first instinct is to go look for where you'd keep a screwdriver in your own home. Is it in the garage? The tool shed? Nope. It's on a table in the sitting room. You just have to wander around aimlessly, scanning every drawer and surface while you wonder if you're missing something that would make this fun. 

The demonic powers are also a little annoying. I could ignore the fact that the telekenisis never feels right, or that the fireballs are basically only available in pre-scripted sections of the game. That stuff, to a degree, makes sense. But the ability to make people forget seeing you doesn't even work! The moment your seen, all of the controls go completely dead, so there's no opportunity to use it. I went so far as intentionally getting caught multiple times in a row just to try and figure out what I was doing wrong, but it's no use. 

The game's cutscenes are too numerous and too boring. And even as numerous as they are, they often fail to explain things. Without spoiling anything, the game's story makes a few strange leaps forward that I still don't really understand. Several characters apparently come out of nowhere. Halfway through the game everyone starts talking about my uncle. Your mom even tells you to stop bothering your uncle, because he's been complaining about you lately. Meanwhile I'm left to wonder who or where my uncle is, because it's the first time I'm hearing about him. 

I'm disappointed that the game wound up being as bland and boring as it is. The graphics are nice and clear, the controls are mostly pretty solid, the deaths are reasonably creative. In most respects the game is a competently assembled thing. But there are just too many problems for me to give it a blanket recommendation. 

I'd say you should buy it only if you meet two criteria:
1. You, like me, think the premise is AWESOME. 
2. It's on sale for less than $3. 

Otherwise, give this a pass.

If you're seeing this review, then you're probably very interested in 'Lucius', a third person action-horror game where you play the son of the devil and go around reaping souls in pretty gruesome ways. While the concept looks good on paper, execution wise the game goes only halfway.
